discussions.item: Public Comment — Boulevard Snow Plowing
discussions.body: Approximately 15 speakers, including residents of Elwood Boulevard, Highland Park Boulevard, Oaklair Boulevard, Everest Boulevard, and Midway Boulevard, testified against the city's current practice of plowing snow to the curb rather than to the center boulevard. Speakers cited safety hazards including blocked driveways, obscured sightlines, inaccessible fire hydrants and sand barrels, and inability of emergency vehicles to pass. Alderperson Carol Lukans (District 1) testified that the boulevard plowing change was never presented as a distinct policy item when the winter maintenance policy was approved unanimously in January 2024, and argued it required separate council approval. Resident Felix Gallow presented a data analysis he said showed returning to center-boulevard plowing would save tens of thousands of dollars annually. Alderperson Lou Larson (District 10) noted a Wisconsin state statute (346.05 sub-2) permits plows to operate against traffic for highway maintenance with proper lighting, and argued no new $40,000 equipment was needed.

discussions.item: Item 4: Boulevard Planting Subcommittee
discussions.body: Alder Wiskowski moved to establish a special exploratory subcommittee to develop a boulevard planting scheme, addressing questions about what plantings — including native plants, pollinator gardens, and possibly vegetable gardens — would be permissible in the right-of-way between street and sidewalk. Alder Lukans raised that the sustainability committee was also working on related issues, prompting a friendly amendment that the subcommittee work in cooperation with the sustainability commission. Engineering staff noted concerns about utility excavation permits disturbing plantings and sightline issues near intersections. The motion as amended carried.

discussions.item: Item 5A: Snowplowing Policy Discussion
discussions.body: Committee members discussed the boulevard plowing issue following public comment. Alder Hanniki and Alder Slonsky both praised the level of citizen engagement and expressed openness to revisiting the policy. Public Works Director Lynman clarified that the department's prior practice of not plowing against traffic came from legal guidance received years ago that a road would need to be closed first, and said he did not intentionally mislead the public. The city attorney confirmed that Wisconsin statute 346.05(2) does appear to allow plowing against traffic with proper lighting, and that the city's insurer would cover such operations, but said a deeper review of administrative codes and DOT requirements was needed. The committee directed staff and the city attorney to return at a future meeting with a formal legal opinion, equipment cost analysis, and multiple costed options for how to address boulevard plowing, but took no formal action at this meeting.

discussions.item: Item 5B: 2027-2030 Infrastructure and Facility Capital Projects
discussions.body: Engineering staff presented the five-year capital infrastructure plan. Alder Hanniki asked for clarification on grant funding assumptions, learning that $600,000 of the $900,000 in 2027 grant funds was tied to the solar array project (likely to be removed after finance committee rejection) and $300,000 was a state reimbursement for East Wausau Avenue right-of-way acquisition rather than a true grant. The committee requested staff add project justification narratives to future capital plan presentations and provide a breakdown identifying legally obligated projects versus discretionary ones.

discussions.item: Item 6: Committee Jurisdiction and Definition of Duties
discussions.body: The committee reviewed a memo from Assistant City Attorney Bonino outlining the Infrastructure and Facilities Committee's statutory duties, including recommending purchase and sale of city real estate for municipal purposes and disposition of underutilized city-owned land. Alder Hanniki and others noted apparent overlap with the Economic Development Committee's jurisdiction over development parcels, and Alder Martin provided historical context that the two committees have informally divided responsibilities. Alder Hanniki proposed a joint meeting between the two committees to clarify boundaries. Alder Wiskowski requested that review of vacant and underutilized city-owned real estate be added to a future committee agenda.

publicComment: Approximately 15 speakers addressed the committee, all focused on the snow plowing policy on boulevard streets. Speakers included: Michael Moran (2513 Elwood Boulevard), who requested return to center-boulevard plowing; Alderperson Lou Larson (904 S. 21st Place, District 10), who cited a state statute allowing wrong-way plowing with proper lighting and challenged the $40,000 equipment cost estimate; Sally Cinto (1220 Highland Park Boulevard), who presented photos showing plows operating 7-8 feet from the curb and blocking access to sand barrels; Mary Broadhead (1101 Highland Park Boulevard), who questioned cost analysis and noted residents receive the full street's worth of snow in their driveways; Jean Krooks (119 Oaklair Boulevard), who described unique traffic challenges on her block; Alderperson Carol Lukans (725 Ethel Street, District 1), who argued the plowing change was implemented without proper council approval and cited Wisconsin statute 346.05(2); Bob Reinardson (1220 Highland Park Boulevard), husband of Sally Cinto, describing street narrowing after reconstruction; a speaker identifying as V. Vleskis (1010 Everest Boulevard), a military retiree describing 7-8 foot snow walls affecting elderly and disabled neighbors; Felix Gallow (1206 Highland Park Boulevard), who presented a data analysis document arguing center-boulevard plowing would save tens of thousands annually; Carrie Mor (1025 Everest Boulevard), who questioned the basis for the $40,000 cost estimate; Karen Briggs (154 Oaklair Boulevard, 51 years resident); Gene Rolki (146 Oaklair Boulevard), who noted a grader with a left plow was previously used and is no longer seen; Kurt Hornby (211 Oaklair Boulevard), who noted fire hydrants relocated to curbside during reconstruction are now buried by snow; Danielle Fischer (1212 Highland Park Boulevard), who noted the neighborhood hosts historic district tours; Jim Wearig (2408 Oakwood Boulevard), who alleged the public works director had lied about the legality of wrong-way plowing; Sarah Esser (2412 Midway Boulevard), who described car damage and missed work due to the snow situation; Kevin Cooper (145 Oaklair Boulevard), who described garbage can and backing-out hazards; Alice Kether (1106 Highland Park Boulevard), who said she has seen blades used to plow to the center without going the wrong way.

discussions.item: Credit union lease at 400 Thomas Street
discussions.body: County administrator reported that the credit union, which leases space at the former social services building at 400 Thomas Street, has not provided a firm move-out date despite multiple requests. Chair Gibbs asked whether the county could invoke the 180-day notice provision in the lease to force the issue. Administrator confirmed the authority exists under the lease. discussions.item: Conduit financing consent via Public Finance Authority for Wasa Hotel Group
discussions.body: County administrator Leonard explained that Wasa Hotel Group requested consent to access up to $10 million in bonding through the Public Finance Authority (PFA) for hotel renovations and debt refinancing, with no financial obligation or impact on the county's general obligation bonding capacity. Managing member John Kofi described the hotel's turnaround from being the second-worst performing Holiday Inn Express out of 2,600 to the top 2%, with $3.5 million invested since 2017 and approximately $285,000 in annual room tax contributions. Bond counsel Frank Gare (Corals and Brady) confirmed there is no statewide cap on PFA issuance. Vice Chair Pool moved to consent; Chair Gibbs seconded. The motion carried unanimously.

discussions.body: Sheriff Chad Phillip and County Administrator Leonard presented detailed data analysis by Data Officer Michael Schultz showing that dedicated Rib Mountain deputies handle only about 29% of calls in the village, with 70-71% handled by non-dedicated county deputies. The data showed peak call volume occurring from noon through early evening, prompting a shift in deputy scheduling toward afternoon hours. Administrator Leonard noted the current contract undercharges Rib Mountain by approximately $30,000 per deputy annually when indirect costs are properly calculated. Vice Chair Pool asked whether the three Rib Mountain deputies also serve other areas; the sheriff confirmed they do, including SWAT, dive team, and crash reconstruction duties, with roughly 60 documented instances of responding outside Rib Mountain. The committee was advised that as a village, Rib Mountain is now legally mandated to provide law enforcement and that any contract requires county board ratification. Further discussion was deferred to closed session.

overview: The Marathon County EEED and HRFC committees held a joint meeting to review four RFP responses for redevelopment of the UW-Stevens Point Wausau campus, plus hear an update on negotiations with the Marathon Center for Arts and Culture. Committees heard presentations from Wisconsin Ice Volleyball Club, the Center for the Visual Arts, Wausau Police Chief Barnes on the City of Wausau's public safety campus proposal, and Parks & Recreation staff before voting unanimously to enter closed session to discuss negotiation strategy on the RFP responses.

discussions.item: RFP Overview — Four Proposals Summarized
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard and Chris Holman presented four RFP responses at a high level, noting this was not a traditional scored RFP but a committee-driven criteria process allowing for negotiation. Holman clarified that the Lone Wolf Works proposal (central heating plant for automotive/fabrication) was essentially a contingency proposal dependent on the heating plant being decommissioned, and was not immediately actionable. A question arose about whether the county could counter-offer; Leonard confirmed further negotiations were anticipated and that any property transfer requires full county board ratification.

discussions.item: Wisconsin Ice Volleyball Club Proposal
discussions.body: Board member Jody Davis explained the club's 25-year history and urgent need for dedicated gym space, citing displacement from Wisconsin Valley Lutheran, scheduling conflicts at Northland Lutheran, and costs of $25–$44/hour at facilities like CTI. Davis clarified that while the proposal included the East and West Arts buildings, the fieldhouse is the club's exclusive priority. The club indicated openness to subletting the pool and other spaces to organizations like the YMCA and youth hockey. In response to a question, Davis confirmed the arts buildings were included to help the county, not because the club needed them.

discussions.item: City of Wausau Proposal — Police Department Campus Relocation
discussions.body: Police Chief Barnes explained the city's motivation: relocating the fire department into the existing police station to avoid an estimated $30–50 million new fire station construction cost, then moving the police department to the UW campus. He described a vision including the Wausau School District potentially occupying the south hall of North-South Hall to address $3 million in deferred maintenance on district offices, and creating a shared regional law enforcement training hub. Barnes emphasized the 6-month due diligence period is to hire third-party experts to assess renovation costs, not a commitment, and stressed the proposal could save taxpayers tens of millions of dollars long-term.

discussions.item: Center for the Visual Arts Proposal
discussions.body: Executive Director Mara Mullen described CVA's 40-year history, 40,000 annual gallery visitors, 90-plus classes per year, and severe space constraints at their downtown location at 427 North Fourth Street — including a two-plus-year camp waitlist and inability to offer oil painting due to ventilation issues. She said the East and West Arts buildings would allow CVA to add a wood shop, print studio, expanded ceramics with a gas kiln, and more youth programming. She noted that building from scratch would cost millions, making the UW campus a highly attractive option, and proposed assuming full operational costs starting January.

discussions.item: Parks Department Community Recreation Proposal
discussions.body: Parks Director Jamie presented a high-level concept for operating the fieldhouse as a county or city community recreation center, with programming including open gyms, leagues, pool use (noting YMCA interest in 5-days-per-week pool rental), county employee fitness center access, senior programming, and potential youth hockey dryland training. She was candid that the facility in its current form would likely require a tax subsidy rather than generate revenue, comparing it to the city's pools. She also flagged that Parks staff currently park in the UW lot and would have no alternative if that lot changed hands.

He said they are discussing interim occupancy mechanisms and that the group may want to accelerate the move-in timeline. He also disclosed that the group informally requested the county act as employer for a new executive director position, fully reimbursed, but noted this raised serious liability concerns and no action was requested at this meeting.

discussions.item: Bushka Park Fundraising Brick Components
discussions.body: Greg (Director of Public Works) presented a fundraising brick program through a company called Gift Bricks, noting that Wastatile agreed to donate all bricks needed and that the etching would be handled by Gift Bricks in southern Wisconsin. The committee agreed to offer three brick sizes — 4x8 at $50, 8x8 at $120, and 8x16 at $250 — representing roughly a 150% markup over cost, with black epoxy fill only for simplicity. The committee discussed advertising at the upcoming 5K, the farmers market, and via QR codes, and agreed to post ordering information on the village website. A motion was made by Patty and seconded by Elizabeth to direct the director of public works to move forward with the brick fundraiser at the agreed sizes and pricing; the motion carried unanimously.

discussions.item: September 12 Bushka Park 5K Run/Walk Fundraiser Event
discussions.body: Mishka reported that all nine police-recommended intersection volunteer positions had been filled with high-visibility vests, and that water bottles and a digital timer clock had been purchased. The start and finish line will be near the shelter at Bushka Park at 10 a.m. Committee members discussed volunteer assignments at intersections, the absence of a rain backup plan ('all weather' event), and the need for a first aid station. A staff member raised the concern that a quorum of trustees attending could constitute a walking quorum, and members were advised to be mindful of that. A donation box with a QR code, created by Kim, will be stationed at the main table.

discussions.item: Capital Improvement Project Costs
discussions.body: Greg presented a 10-year CIP list including: Bushka Park playground ($200,000), Norm Plaza Dog Park fencing ($50,000), Friendship Park rubberized surfacing ($80,000, 2029), a bandstand and bathrooms ($150,000), and Municipal Park bathrooms ($100,000). Significant debate arose over the Municipal Park bathroom, with Tim arguing the remote location, high maintenance costs, vandalism risk, and distance from water and sewer made it a poor investment, while other members countered that a disc golf course at that site would increase usage and justify the facility. Greg noted staff prefer porter potties due to vandalism and maintenance issues. The committee agreed to keep the bathroom line item but defer the decision, and also agreed to add the disc golf course to the quick fix/future list. A motion by Dan to recommend the capital improvement plan as presented to the village board was seconded and carried unanimously.

discussions.item: Quick Fix Item List
discussions.body: Greg reviewed completed and in-progress quick fix items, including power washing playground equipment, ordering a replacement slide for North Plaza, ordering inclusive swings, and updating park signage to reflect current ordinances. A committee member asked that park benches along walking trails be added to the list. Greg confirmed the broken globe piece at Bushka Park is on order and that the volleyball net at Smith Park has not yet been installed. Greg also noted he would investigate a boundary encroachment concern at Towering Pines park involving bike path users the following day using GIS.

discussions.item: Friendship Park Zipline
discussions.body: Mishka proposed using approximately $20,000 in savings from the reduced wellhead trail project to install a zipline at Friendship Park, citing a price of roughly $20,000 and noting it could boost community excitement and generate positive press for park fundraising. Greg confirmed there is adequate space at Friendship Park. Members debated whether the expenditure would undermine Bushka Park fundraising momentum, with some arguing it would signal village investment in parks while others felt Bushka Park should remain the clear priority. The committee ultimately declined to fund a zipline immediately due to uncertainty about trail project final costs and the desire to focus on Bushka Park, but Dan moved to add the zipline to the 2029 Friendship Park CIP line, increasing that budget from $80,000 to $100,000. The motion was seconded by Tim and carried unanimously. The committee also discussed the ADA accessibility advantage of using the bucket seat option on the zipline, which costs approximately $1,000 more.

discussions.item: Consideration of Items for Future Agenda
discussions.body: Members discussed the uncertain future of the 'Friends of the Parks' volunteer fundraising group, noting that the staff member who had been organizing it (Jennifer) is no longer with the village and little progress appears to have been made. Members discussed whether the CLIP committee would absorb parks oversight in the interim, with Dan and Patty both serving on CLIP. Members expressed interest in reviving the Friends of the Parks effort, possibly tied to Saturday's 5K event as a recruitment opportunity. A brief discussion occurred about committee compensation being deposited into the general parks fund rather than specifically to Bushka Park donations, with Greg clarifying it goes to the overall parks fund and could be redirected by committee vote with board approval.

overview: The Marathon County Public Safety Committee met on September 8, 2026, and covered several significant topics including a Valor Award presentation to Deputy Edward Alt-Bneck for stopping a dangerous pursuit, an overview of the Recreation Deputy partnership between the Sheriff's Office and Parks & Recreation, radio paging challenges in rural areas, and a detailed discussion of the Rib Mountain law enforcement services contract. discussions.item: Valor Award Presentation to Deputy Edward Alt-Bneck
discussions.body: The Sheriff presented the Sheriff's Office Valor Award to Deputy Edward Alt-Bneck (known informally as 'Sheriff Eddie') for his actions on August 5th during a 24-minute pursuit of an attempted homicide suspect. The Sheriff described how Deputy Alt-Bneck used his patrol vehicle to execute a ram maneuver — classified as a deadly force decision — to stop the fleeing suspect on Meer Street, putting himself in significant personal danger. The Sheriff noted Alt-Bneck was hospitalized afterward and that his first words upon being called were 'Sorry about your car.' Lieutenant Matt Bell was credited with authorizing the use of the ram. The committee applauded the deputy.

discussions.item: Recreation Deputy Program Overview
discussions.body: Parks, Recreation & Forestry Director Jamie Py presented the county's Recreation Deputy program, which has been operating since 2020 and was highlighted at a national parks conference in Phoenix. The program embeds Sheriff's Office deputies — currently Brian Majeski and Ethan Burmeister — into the parks department to patrol 38 city parks, 17 county parks, and 10 county forest units, funded through the parks budget at one FTE. Py noted the program has increased compliance, improved camper safety perceptions, driven ordinance updates, and has been popular enough that eight strong internal candidates applied for the most recent opening. Committee members expressed support, and County Administrator Leonard praised it as a model for other intergovernmental partnerships.

discussions.item: Central Wisconsin Community Mediation – 2027 Budget Presentation
discussions.body: Randy Westgate, director of Community Mediation of Wisconsin (which absorbed the program from Judicare/Legal Action), presented results of the $15,000 annual county contract. He reported that in the past year, 865 of 1,029 contested small claims cases (84%) were resolved without trial, including a 97% resolution rate for eviction cases. Westgate emphasized the program prevents homelessness and saves an estimated $60,000 in court time annually. Administrator Leonard indicated funding would remain at $15,000 for 2027, but Westgate signaled the 2028 request would likely be $20,000. No action was taken; the item was informational.

discussions.item: Radio Paging Quality Challenges – Edgar, Hamburg, Texas
discussions.body: Sheriff Bilip and Captain Berdall presented two options to address paging dead zones in the Village of Edgar, Town of Hamburg, and Town of Texas: a $500,000–$520,000 infrastructure fix (new tower at Bug Tussle site) versus a pilot of the G2 app at $15 per user per year (approximately $720 annually for Edgar). The Sheriff and Administrator Leonard strongly recommended the G2 pilot, which simultaneously pushes call information via pager, the G2 app, and the 'I Am Responding' app. Captain Berdall confirmed the Edgar fire chief has provided a list of firefighters to begin the pilot. Radio tech Kellen Stouse addressed a question from Supervisor [inaudible] about satellite communications, explaining that public-safety satellite systems are not yet viable but may be in 10–20 years with Starlink-type technology. No formal vote was taken; this was an informational update.

discussions.item: Year-to-Date Budget Reports
discussions.body: Finance staff member Sam reported all public safety departments are within their payroll benchmark of 46.74% and operating budgets are on track. The one area being monitored is a projected $130,000 revenue shortfall in the District Attorney's office due to a state-level change in discovery fee rules — the state public defender's office dramatically reduced what it will pay for discovery. Administrator Leonard noted DA Mayo is working with the DA association and the Wisconsin Counties Association lobbyist on a potential state-level fix. Supervisor [inaudible] asked about remaining ARPA funds; Leonard and Sam confirmed approximately $480,824 remains unspent of the original $26,356,580 award, with roughly $200,000 expected to be reallocated to a previously approved project before year-end.

discussions.item: Rib Mountain Law Enforcement Services Contract Review
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard and Sheriff Bilip presented data showing that Rib Mountain-assigned deputies handle only about 29.2% of calls for service in the village, with non-assigned deputies covering the remaining ~71%. The county has provided law enforcement to Rib Mountain since 2020; since 2023, Rib Mountain (now a village) is legally required to have law enforcement. Three deputies are currently assigned to Rib Mountain, with a fourth planned. Sam reported those three deputies cost just under $400,000 from January 2024 to January 2025. The committee discussed the service-level implications of pulling deputies from other sectors to cover Rib Mountain calls, with Chair Gibbs asking about the volume of case numbers generated (estimated ~1,600 per year). Administrator Leonard noted the levy to support the sheriff's department grows faster than net new construction, making cost-recovery agreements like this one financially important. The committee prepared to move into closed session to continue contract negotiations discussion.

discussions.item: Sustainability, Energy, and Environment Committee Presentation
discussions.body: Committee representative Jesse Karns presented an update on the committee's work toward a five-year sustainability action plan, expected to be finalized and presented to council in April 2027. Karns highlighted a community survey launched September 1 and running through October 31, outreach at Artfest, a composting demonstration partnership with SUS, a Wausau Sustainability Award to be presented during Earth Week, and the city's 2023 resolution to achieve 100% clean energy for city government by 2050. discussions.body: The resolution came to the council after being voted down unanimously in the Infrastructure and Facilities Committee. Alders Slansky, Neil, Trueblood, and Martins all spoke against it, arguing that a permanent easement would limit future redevelopment flexibility on a parcel where active negotiations are reportedly underway. Martins noted the city has owned the property since 2006 and that outdoor advertising is scarce, making a continued lease more advantageous. The motion failed 0-11.

discussions.item: File 06906: DPW Organizational Structure Changes and Succession Planning
discussions.body: Public Works Director Eric Lynman was invited to the podium by Council President Terry Kilian, who asked him to confirm on the record that proposed utility fee increases were not a dependency of this reorganization proposal — Lynman confirmed the changes are within the current budget. Alder Watson noted the reorganization appeared to be ahead of a pending broader organizational study. Alder Heni asked about whether elimination of a part-time facilities position would affect winter plowing capacity; Lynman confirmed plowing remains the top priority. Alder Larson asked how the changes would benefit citizens and whether the Murphy Report had informed them; Lynman said some Mercury Report suggestions had already been implemented. Mayor Diny noted succession planning is a goal for all nine department directors. The motion passed 10-1, with Alder Larson indicating he would withhold his vote pending a city audit.

discussions.item: File 260918: Reclassification of HR Specialist to HR Generalist
discussions.body: Multiple alders spoke in strong support, with Wiscowski, Slansky, Tyranny, Martins, and Larson all noting the employee has long been performing generalist-level duties while paid at the specialist rate, and that the HR department is critically understaffed — described as currently a department of two while structured for four. Alder Trueblood raised a concern that while the $40,760 in savings covers the reclassification cost in 2026, it will be a permanent ongoing budget impact in future years. Alder Heni asked for clarification on the precise salary amount, which the interim HR director confirmed as the resolution amount. The motion passed 11-0.

discussions.item: File 260921: Lead and Galvanized Water Service Line Replacement Ordinance
discussions.body: This item generated the longest and most contentious debate of the evening. DPW Director Eric Lynman explained the city has replaced over 500 lines in 2024, 1,500 in 2025, and is on track for 1,700 in 2026, with an EPA deadline of 2037. Council President Kilian said she would not support it because residents were initially told there would be no fees. Alder Slansky supported it to qualify for future grants but asked that costs be spread equitably. Alder Trueblood drew a contrast with the evening's pending $28 million Riverlife development agreement and argued the city had overpromised on the no-cost pledge. Alder Watson raised questions about circular logic between the ordinance and funding, and asked whether enforcement could be tied to funding availability. Alder Heni moved to amend the ordinance to prohibit penalties, enforcement, and water disconnection until the council adopts a financing program defining maximum obligations, repayment terms, and hardship considerations; Alder Tyranny seconded. After extended debate on whether that amendment could jeopardize PSC approval or grant eligibility, Heni withdrew the amendment without objection. Alder Larson called the question to end debate on the main motion. The ordinance ultimately passed, though the exact tally was not clearly stated in the transcript before the recording ended.

publicComment: Two speakers offered public comment. David Rele, 1200 North Mayfair Road, Milwaukee, spoke in support of the Riverlife/Wongard development agreement, thanking the council for the opportunity and stating the development agreement captures all form and function approved in the prior term sheet. A second speaker, identified as Apple Quizzler (address given as 417 Lazy Branch Drive, Wausau), spoke about 911 access and cellular service reliability problems in the Lazy Acres neighborhood (approximately 190 homes). The speaker described spotty cellular coverage and a situation where a satellite app appearing on their phone appeared to interfere with cellular service, blocking the ability to call 911. Mayor Diny indicated city staff would follow up with the resident.

overview: The Village of Weston Board of Trustees and Finance/HR Committee held a joint budget workshop covering the 2027 preliminary budget, including wage and benefit analysis, general fund breakdown, special revenue funds, and a discussion of potential modified summer hours. No final budget decisions were made, as the board has three more budget workshops remaining before an end-of-October deadline; the primary formal action taken was reclassifying an engineering technician from FLSA-exempt to non-exempt status, with retroactive effect to his July 6 start date.

discussions.item: Public Comments
discussions.body: Three residents spoke. A woman identified as Grace (603 Jessica, Weston) raised concerns about the proposed Friday afternoon closures and asked that overtime calculations for reclassified hourly employees be based on a 40-hour workweek, not eight hours per day; staff confirmed Weston uses the over-40-hours standard. Jim Pel criticized the lack of a clear, readable answer to a previously requested 1%-salary-impact figure, argued against closing Village Hall on Fridays as inequitable to public-facing departments, and suggested extended evening hours instead; he also complained the PowerPoint was not in the packet until the day of the meeting. A third resident, John of 1506 Daily Avenue, questioned why a Weston ordinance required a licensed plumber to replace an anti-siphon faucet rather than allowing a homeowner to do it themselves.

discussions.item: Approval of August 24, 2026 Joint Budget Workshop Minutes
discussions.body: The Finance/HR Committee approved the minutes on a motion by Daniels, seconded by [inaudible]. The Board of Trustees approved the same minutes on a motion by Beck, seconded by Ermeling. Both votes carried without dissent.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Review: Wage and Benefit Analysis
discussions.body: Finance staff presented slides showing that a 1% wage increase costs approximately $17,583 in the general fund, with the caveat that the calculation excludes elected officials and election workers who receive no scheduled increases, causing confusion when trustees tried to verify the math. Trustee Christina [inaudible] noted the numbers did not 'math out' and requested that future spreadsheets include contextual notes or assumptions. Staff explained that the benefit figures also incorporate a preliminary 10% health insurance increase and WRS cost increases, making a straight 1% calculation misleading. Village Administrator [inaudible] and Finance Director Jessica defended releasing complex data at the meeting rather than in advance to prevent misinterpretation, while trustees pushed back, saying advance access is necessary for informed deliberation. Both sides acknowledged the tension and agreed future budget documents would include explanatory notes.

discussions.item: General Fund Breakdown and Transportation Aids
discussions.body: Staff presented the $9.6 million 2026 general fund, noting that roughly 55% is locked in public safety contracts with Mountain Bay and South Area Fire (SAFER), leaving the board meaningful discretion over only about $3.3 million. Administrator Michael [inaudible] explained that transportation aid revenue rose significantly after years of steep annual declines from roughly 2012–2021, driven by reduced infrastructure spending in TIF districts, but warned the aid formula is expected to plateau or decline again around 2030–2031. Trustees were cautioned not to commit transportation aid dollars to non-transportation purposes. Staff also used the Wisconsin Policy Forum's municipal comparison tool to show Weston has among the lowest general government expenditures and property tax levy per capita compared to neighboring communities, and is second-lowest in shared revenue per capita in the comparison group. The village's Moody's bond rating of Aa3 (issued August 2026) was noted as solid, constrained partly by Marathon County's Aa2 ceiling.

discussions.item: Special Revenue Funds
discussions.body: Staff reviewed six special revenue funds. The refuse/recycling fund is projected to draw down its $156,000 fund balance by approximately $62,000 in 2026 due to unexpected diesel fuel surcharges under the Harder's contract; staff indicated the $25.50 resident fee may need to increase to $27.10 for 2027, pending August data. The aquatic center fund is projected to roughly break even or gain $8,000 in 2026 after fee increases ($5 to $7 daily, higher season passes boosted revenues despite lower attendance); a $100,000 capital borrowing placeholder was included for a pool leak repair whose actual cost is still unknown. TIF District No. 1 is closing, with a roughly $400,000 one-time levy adjustment expected; approximately $1.95 million is being held to retire CDA lease revenue bond debt. TIF District No. 2 (Schofield Avenue) carries a roughly $470,000 deficit projected through end of 2027 after the state slashed assessed value in early 2025. Room tax: the village's 30% share produced about $197,000 to the Weston account in 2025 out of $461,000 paid to the CVB; the fund balance is growing to approximately $230,000 through Q2 and staff flagged it must be spent on tourism purposes before the next two-year CVB agreement renewal in 2027. The Civic, Social and Park Trust fund will resume $500 scholarships through DC Everest for the first time in years, funded by improved CD interest rates (approximately 4.01%).

discussions.item: FLSA Reclassification of Engineering Technician
discussions.body: Public Works Director Michael [inaudible] explained that a newly hired engineering technician serving as on-site inspector for the Concord A project had been incorrectly classified as FLSA-exempt (salaried) since his July 6 hire date. The Finance/HR Committee and board both voted to reclassify the position to non-exempt (hourly) retroactive to July 6, 2026. Staff estimated the retroactive overtime owed is less than $1,000 in wages, and noted the position generates significant savings versus contracting out inspection at roughly $120/hour compared to approximately $30–35/hour in-house. The Finance/HR Committee voted first, then the Board of Trustees adopted a corresponding motion.

discussions.item: Potential Modified Summer Hours for 2027
discussions.body: Village President Maloney introduced a discussion on potentially adopting a compressed summer schedule (e.g., Monday–Thursday extended hours with a half-day Friday) similar to neighboring municipalities: Rothschild, Kronenwetter, and Schofield operate 7 a.m.–4:30 p.m. Monday–Thursday and 7–11 a.m. Friday; Rib Mountain does 7:30–5 and 8:30–1; Wausau uses Monday/Wednesday/Thursday 7:30–4:30 with a late Tuesday and half-day Friday. Staff clarified that public works already runs four 10-hour days (Memorial Day–Labor Day) and would be unaffected. Utilities and parks staff would also be excluded. Staff noted a prior attempt at modified hours generated employee and public complaints about early start times and reduced Friday access. Two public commenters had already expressed opposition (Pel) and partial concern (Grace). No decision was made; the topic was deferred to future budget workshops for further discussion.

publicComment: Three residents spoke. Grace (603 Jessica, Weston) raised concerns about equity in overtime calculations if staff are reclassified hourly, and asked the village to ensure hourly employees are paid only for actual hours worked. Jim Pel criticized the absence of a clear answer to the 1%-salary-cost question, opposed closing Village Hall on Fridays as inequitable to non-administrative departments, suggested extended evening hours as an alternative, and complained the budget PowerPoint was not in the meeting packet until the day of the meeting. John (1506 Daily Avenue) questioned a village ordinance requiring a licensed plumber to replace an anti-siphon faucet on his 1960 home, questioning why the work could not be done by a homeowner with a receipt showing a new part.

title: Community Life & Public Safety
overview: The Village of Weston Community Life & Public Safety Committee met on September 8th to address overnight parking regulations for winter snow removal, animal fancier license standards, and code enforcement updates. The committee approved a recommendation to the village board to modify the winter overnight parking ordinance, adding alternating-day parking restrictions on six high-density streets from October 31st to May 1st. The animal fancier license size standards discussion was tabled pending input from a humane officer at the next meeting.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Jim Pinsenalt of PC Street West addressed the committee with two concerns. First, he expressed alarm that code enforcement cases are rising while the village board was simultaneously considering reducing building hours and granting additional paid holidays to staff, questioning how existing cases could be handled under those conditions. Second, he argued that the animal fancier license ordinance lacks specific standards for dogs and other animals, noting that guidelines exist for chickens but not for dogs or cats, and called for defined minimums for space, food, water, shelter, and outdoor exercise areas to enable fact-based rather than feelings-based decisions.

discussions.item: Code Enforcement Update
discussions.body: Staff noted that the increase in August code enforcement cases was largely attributable to grass complaints following the end of a drought period. The committee discussed the ongoing situation at 4020 Scoffield Avenue, with staff reporting that Lock Reinvestments had been in contact and was preparing new plans for dumpster enclosures for the entire property; once approved by staff and their hauler Harters, permits would be entered into the system at no charge and work was expected to be completed that fall. Staff also raised the ongoing issue of violation notice letters taking up to 10 days to reach residents, exceeding the required response windows, and noted that staff was working to address this through email outreach and planned ordinance review during the slower winter months.

discussions.item: Police and Fire Department Monthly Reports
discussions.body: Police Chief Hunt reported that calls for service stood at approximately 2,367, with traffic citations at 311 and traffic stops at 437, describing numbers as consistent and stable. He noted that citations would increase slightly with school back in session, and that traffic crashes were up slightly to 60. The chief also reported that skate park calls for service had been down compared to prior years, attributed informally to the prevalence of e-scooters and e-bikes, and that e-moto enforcement had resulted in at least one tow and citations with cooperative parents. A question was raised about the 'other' category in the fire response report, which could not be answered and was flagged for follow-up at the next SAFER board meeting.

discussions.item: Overnight Parking Regulations (Section 82.107)
discussions.body: Staff member Michael presented a revised proposal to reduce the number of streets with alternating-day parking restrictions from over a dozen to six high-density locations, primarily near apartment complexes like Foxrun, where snow plows have historically been unable to pass due to cars parked on both sides. After extensive discussion, the committee agreed on a uniform 2:00 a.m. to 7:00 a.m. no-parking restriction on all village streets to align with neighboring municipalities, plus alternating-day restrictions (Monday/Wednesday/Friday/Sunday on one side, Tuesday/Thursday/Saturday on the other) on the six listed streets from 7:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The police chief expressed a preference for overnight enforcement as officers are less busy then, and noted tickets are approximately $10. A committee member also requested that ordinance language be added to formalize the process by which streets are added to the restricted list, requiring justification and committee/board approval. A motion was made and passed to recommend these changes to the village board, including sign cost estimated at just over $2,000.

discussions.item: Animal Fancier License Size and Configuration Requirements (Section 10-123)
discussions.body: Trustee Brent raised this item following a recent animal fancier permit denial by the village board, where a lack of specific size standards in the ordinance created difficulty in the decision-making process. Chief Hunt strongly advised against adding detailed size requirements, arguing the ordinance's current subjectivity allows humane officers to use professional judgment, and that setting explicit standards could invite more applications and reduce enforcement flexibility. He noted 18 calls for service at the property in question from May through August. Staff noted that the humane officers receive specialized training through UW-Madison's veterinary school. The committee agreed to table the ordinance amendment discussion and invite one or more humane officers to a future meeting to provide education on what standards they apply, before deciding whether changes are needed.

discussions.item: Code Enforcement Follow-up: 1706 Newport Avenue
discussions.body: A committee member reported homework assigned at the prior meeting regarding citations issued at 1706 Newport Avenue, a chronic nuisance/hoarding property. Citations totaling $4,145 were issued to one resident (with $1,300 remaining delinquent) and $2,656 to another (with $969 remaining delinquent), across 38 citations dating back to 2022. Staff noted 47 total cases at that address going back to 2008, and that staff invested 15–18 hours on the most recent case alone. The property has been cleaned up three times through non-summary abatement, with costs including dumpster rental billed to the property and subject to tax intercept if unpaid. Staff noted that administrative fees were added to bills this cycle for the first time to begin recouping staff time costs, and discussed the contrast with cities like Oshkosh that charge $50 per enforcement letter sent.

publicComment: One speaker offered public comment: Jim Pinsenalt of PC Street West. He raised two issues: (1) concern that rising code enforcement cases were incompatible with a proposal before the board to reduce building hours and add paid holidays for staff, and (2) a call for the committee to establish defined size, sanitation, food, water, and outdoor exercise standards for the animal fancier license ordinance, noting that standards exist for chickens but not for dogs or other animals.

discussions.body: Kim Weber, executive director of McDevco, presented on McDevco's three pillars: educate, incubate, and finance. She reported the Wausau Business Incubator is now 93% full (up from 61% post-COVID), with manufacturing at 100% capacity. She noted McDevco has deployed the full $1 million in Marathon County revolving loan funds, with lending approaching $1 million in 2024. McDevco receives $40,000 annually from Marathon County for educational programming. A supervisor asked about agricultural loan demand; Weber said most farm-related activity involves septic system loans rather than business expansion loans. Another supervisor asked about the microloan default rate; Weber reported approximately 0.12%. The administrator indicated the plan absent contrary direction is to continue funding McDevco in 2027 at prior levels.

discussions.item: LifeWorks Program — Advance Wisconsin Employment (taken out of order)
discussions.body: Brian Kish, executive director of Advance Wisconsin Employment, and Amy Hopa, program operations manager, presented the LifeWorks pilot program targeting justice-involved individuals for manufacturing workforce placement. The pilot cohort of six referrals saw three participants successfully complete three weeks of training including move-to-manufacturing skills at NTC, with employer tours and guaranteed interviews scheduled at Wausau Tile, Green Heck, Crystal Finishing, and Schooty Metals. Kish requested $25,000 annually from the county to fund quarterly cohorts at approximately $12,000 each. Committee members raised questions about legal authority to fund such a program, KPI reporting requirements, whether funding could be structured as a match with participating manufacturers, and whether the program was regional or Marathon County-specific (Kish confirmed funds would be designated for Marathon County). Corporation Counsel Desmond cautioned that statutory restrictions may limit the county's legal authority to fund the program. Administrator Leonard referenced a prior committee allocation process and suggested re-establishing a competitive application process. The committee directed staff to evaluate legal authority, feasibility, and potential KPI and match structures and report back.

discussions.item: Greater Wausau Prosperity Partnership — WEDC Talent Recruitment Grant Update
discussions.body: Renee Kings, senior director of GWPP, reported that GWPP was selected as one of 17 recipients of a WEDC talent recruitment grant, receiving $500,000 — the largest award tied with one other community — out of a statewide $5 million investment. The program aims to recruit 30 out-of-state households to the greater Wausau region by providing a $10,000 relocation grant, personalized relocation support, and community integration services. Eligibility requires residing outside Wisconsin at application, combined household income of at least $55,000, and relocation within six months of acceptance. A supervisor asked about recapture provisions if the 24-month residency commitment is not met; Kings confirmed there is no financial recapture provision but that quarterly check-ins and employer reporting are planned. The program website was previewed and is set to launch the following week.

discussions.item: UW Extension Monthly Report
discussions.body: Jen (last name not stated) provided monthly reports for June, July, and August. Highlights included a successful county fair, a youth summer theater camp with over 40 enrollees, and the conclusion of three AmeriCorps staff terms with one returning. She noted UW Extension expert Bill McKen has been providing information on joint development agreements to a local work group and that a community resilience workshop on green infrastructure was held that day with staff from Marathon, Portage, Waupaca, and Wood counties. No questions or concerns were raised by committee members.

discussions.item: UWSP Wausau Report
discussions.body: Miranda (last name not stated) reported that UWSP Wausau held its first day of classes at the new NTC location, with students successfully finding the new site. UWSP signage has been removed from the Marathon County campus to avoid student confusion, except at the Center for Civic Engagement which continues programming. Enrollment is slightly down as expected during the transition, with official 10th-day figures to be presented at the October meeting. Miranda noted ongoing coordination with the county on items to be left behind for future occupants.

discussions.item: Year-to-Date Budget Reports
discussions.body: Sam (last name not stated) reported no concerns in either the library or UW Extension budgets. The library is at 93.1% of non-levy revenue budget and under its payroll benchmark, with overall expenditures at 43.2% of budget. UW Extension expenditures are anticipated to come in below budget due to a vacancy, with a corresponding reduction in donations revenue. A coding discrepancy in the professional services line was noted as a budget transfer issue with no fiscal concern.

discussions.item: RFP Proposals for UWSP Marathon County Campus — City of Wausau Proposal
discussions.body: Randy Fifick, representing the City of Wausau, presented the city's proposal requesting a six-month due diligence and planning option before committing to acquisition. He noted that a budget modification to fund architectural, engineering, and environmental studies was delayed due to a lack of quorum at the August council meeting and would be introduced at the next meeting. Supervisor Robinson asked whether the proposal was divisible (specifically regarding the dormitory demolition), whether the city could provide an early exit clause if feasibility is determined sooner than six months, and whether the city would cover holding costs during the study period. Fifick indicated all items are negotiable but noted that industry practice would have the existing property owner (the county) bear holding costs, drawing a pointed response about the county's fiscal constraints. Committee members also raised questions about parking allocation and the central heating plant operation relative to multiple potential tenants.

discussions.item: RFP Proposals — Wisconsin Ice Volleyball Club and Other Proposals
discussions.body: Zod Davis, representing Wisconsin Ice Volleyball Club, joined by phone and proposed either purchasing three buildings for $5 each ($15 total) or leasing all three buildings and parking lots for $540 annually for a minimum of five years, with the club covering utilities and snow removal. Davis emphasized the fieldhouse meets all their needs for a nine-month-per-year program drawing players from a wide regional area. Chris (staff, last name not stated) summarized the Lone Wolf Works proposal for the central heating plant, which proposed a $75,000 purchase for conversion to a small automotive restoration and custom fabrication business, with no external financing required. Staff noted CVA could not attend but would present at the HR Finance and Property Committee meeting the following week. The proposals were noted as not scored in a traditional RFP sense per county board direction, but evaluated against criteria established in the RFP document.

title: Infrastructure Committee Meeting Pt.1
overview: The Marathon County Infrastructure Committee met to discuss the Bug Tussle broadband project, which faces a significant scope modification because insufficient bond funds remain to complete the originally planned fiber loop. Bug Tussle representatives presented updates on current infrastructure, BEAD program awards, and marketing efforts before the committee voted to enter closed session to deliberate on the proposed scope change, potential litigation, and a new $45-50 million bonding request. The meeting is significant to residents because the southern fiber loop — a key component of the original broadband expansion agreement — is unlikely to be completed as planned.

discussions.body: A man identified as chairman of the Town of Ringle addressed the committee about deteriorating pavement on the access road to the county salt shed off Highway 29 on Duncan Road. He described the road as 'alligatored' and noted the worst damage occurs where trucks turn toward the loading ramp, likely due to salt spillage. discussions.body: A motion to approve the minutes was made by Sarah [last name inaudible] and seconded by Tom [last name inaudible]. The motion carried unanimously.

discussions.item: Bug Tussle Broadband Project — Infrastructure Status Presentation
discussions.body: Bug Tussle representatives — including George [Quins], Avery Shelbine, and Chris Hverson appearing virtually — presented current project status: 206 live fiber miles in Marathon County, 16 fixed wireless sites deployed, 19 multi-purpose towers, and approximately 5,800 locations passable by fixed wireless and 2,800 by fiber. They noted the original plan called for 288 miles of fiber; the current plan will deliver approximately 281 miles by year-end after completing 74 additional miles, with the southern loop (~45 miles) being dropped as financially infeasible due to insufficient homes along the route. Outstanding construction segments include the Huitt Tower (2.7 miles), Stratford Water Tower (7.19 miles), Hatley/East Side Sheriff's Tower (4.5 miles), and Brokaw East (3.86 miles), all contracted to United Electric for fall 2024 construction.

discussions.item: Subscription/Take Rate Decline
discussions.body: Supervisor Aaron Griner questioned why subscription rates had declined from the June presentation — fixed fiber service from 4.15% to 2.99% and fixed wireless from 5.19% to 1.37%. Bug Tussle's Avery Shelbine attributed the decline partly to customer churn (subscribers moving to faster Bug Tussle fiber plans or SpaceX) and partly to a recalculation of the total addressable market using updated engineering assessments, which significantly increased the denominator for the take-rate calculation. George [Quins] acknowledged that Bug Tussle had not focused adequately on marketing during the construction phase and described new sales and digital marketing efforts now underway.

discussions.item: Scope Modification — Southern Loop Removal and County Board Approval
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson and County Attorney Jerry Klene led substantive discussion about whether the elimination of the southern fiber loop constitutes a formal scope change requiring county board approval. Klene stated Bug Tussle was told as early as a January meeting in Green Bay that dropping the southern loop would require board approval, and this was reiterated before the June educational meeting. Administrator Lance Leonard confirmed there are insufficient project funds remaining to complete the original scope and directed Bug Tussle to produce a formal addendum comparing the original bond issuance documents to the revised scope, including exact mileage differences, for a future committee review. Supervisor Guy asked whether microwave transmission could serve as an adequate substitute for the southern loop; Klene said it would not be ideal but could be made functional if Stratford Water Tower, Huitt Tower, and the east tower connections are completed to provide redundancy for public safety.

discussions.item: Bug Tussle Future Bonding Request
discussions.body: George Quins briefly outlined a proposed new bond in the range of $45-50 million, described as primarily supporting the BEAD program match requirements, expanded fiber passings, marketing and sales investment, and refinancing of existing financial commitments. He indicated the bond would be structured as a multi-county instrument shared across Bug Tussle's partner counties in Wisconsin. Detailed financials were reserved for the closed session.

discussions.body: Administrator Leonard and County Attorney Brian [last name inaudible] recommended closed session to discuss scope modification details, litigation risk, and Bug Tussle's confidential financial projections. title: Committee of the Whole Meeting
committee: City of Wausau Committee of the Whole
overview: The Wausau Committee of the Whole met on September 2, 2026 to consider a proposal by Alders Heni and True Blood to commission a comprehensive, independent systemic audit of city government. After an extensive presentation and discussion, the committee unanimously approved a motion directing the executive committee to develop a scope of work, procurement process, and timeline for the audit, with the full proposal to return to the common council for approval before any contract is awarded. The meeting also addressed growing public concern about city financial reporting accuracy, including a reported $14 million discrepancy in motorpool fund history tables, a $36 million sewer debt understatement, and a material weakness flagged by external auditors tied to a $1 million prior period adjustment.

discussions.item: Public Comment on Agenda Items
discussions.body: Three speakers addressed the council. Joanne Leonard (923 Maple Hill Road), a former Marathon County Board member and retired Wisconsin Public Service manager, called for a comprehensive financial audit by outside experts, criticizing what she described as inadequate financial controls and expressed opposition to the mayor's alternative plan. Liz Hower (1106 North Third Street) called for an independent audit conducted by a firm with no prior ties to the city, citing the need for transparency and accountability. Deborah Ryan (702 Elm Street), a former alder (2020–2022) and retired accountant, raised a series of specific historical financial concerns including an allegedly unauthorized $5,000 legal opinion obtained by a former finance director, an unrecorded housing authority loan, vendor contracts signed without required authorization, and incomplete records requests; she called for the finance director to be relieved of daily duties.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes of Preceding Committee of the Whole Meeting (July 13, 2026)
discussions.body: Alder Larson moved to approve the minutes as presented; Alder Lukans seconded. The motion passed on a voice vote with no opposition.

discussions.item: Presentation: Comprehensive Independent Systemic Audit
discussions.body: Alders Heni and True Blood jointly presented a detailed proposal for a citywide systemic audit, explicitly framing it as not a forensic audit and not intended to assign blame or uncover wrongdoing. Heni cited specific financial reporting concerns including a $14 million discrepancy in motorpool fund budget history tables over 10 years, a $36 million understatement of sewer debt in published schedules, and a material weakness identified by the city's own independent auditors linked to a $1 million prior period adjustment reported the same day. True Blood emphasized structural inefficiencies, including equipment and staff whose purposes are unclear, outdated organizational practices unchanged since the 1960s, a lack of meaningful exit interview processes, and the city hiring outside contractors at higher rates than employees for work existing departments are supposed to perform.

discussions.item: Discussion of Motion as Amended
discussions.body: Multiple council members expressed support while raising concerns about implementation. Alders Slonski and Drew cautioned that audit findings might reveal the need for additional spending — including new staff, software, or equipment — rather than yielding tax savings, and urged clear public communication about realistic timelines for implementing changes. Alder Martins noted the prior Mercury motorpool study took over six to eight months and its recommendations were largely unimplemented due to levy limits and expenditure restraint, warning the same constraints could hinder this audit's outcomes. Alder Larson asked whether the audit would cover the potential purchase of the old WMC/NTC campus for police and fire, and was told the audit was intended to work in tandem with normal city functions rather than halt them. Mayor Doug Diny stated the city would continue normal operations and cited ongoing improvements already underway, including new budget presentation formats with bar charts for the 2027 budget. Absent Alder Tierney's written statement was read aloud, expressing strong support for the audit and stating her first preference would actually be a forensic audit; Alder Watson's written statement was noted as in the packet but not read at her request.

discussions.item: Motion to Direct Alder Heni to Prepare All-Staff Memo
discussions.body: Following passage of the main motion, Alder Lukans moved to direct Alder Heni to prepare a concise memo to all city staff — including fire and police — summarizing the evening's discussion and inviting them to the future council meeting where the audit proposal will be considered. Alder Slonski seconded. A brief procedural question was raised about whether the motion was germane to the agenda; the presiding officer indicated she had confirmed with the city attorney it would be, and Alder Heni volunteered to write the memo regardless of the vote. The motion passed on a voice vote with no opposition.

title: Health and Human Services Committee Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Health and Human Services Committee held its regular meeting, receiving budget presentations from North Central Community Action Program, United Way of Marathon County (211 services), and the ADRC of Central Wisconsin, all of which highlighted growing financial pressures amid flat or reduced funding streams. The committee also received a quarterly update on the county-city homelessness response foundational framework and a preview of the strategic plan survey process. No significant funding changes were approved; the ADRC's requested levy increase was confirmed as already built into the 2027 budget.

discussions.body: Minutes were moved and seconded without discussion. The chair called for a voice vote and the motion carried.

discussions.item: North Central Community Action Program - 2027 Budget Presentation
discussions.body: Executive Director Diane Senholtz presented CAP's 2025 impact in Marathon County: $2.6 million in goods and services including weatherization of 130 homes, emergency furnace repairs for 100 households, crisis rental payments of $289,000 for 681 households, and $300,000 in transitional housing for 10 households. Administrator Leonard noted the county's annual funding of $33,757 is used as match to leverage additional federal and state dollars, and stated his plan is to fund North Central CAP at the same level as prior years absent committee direction otherwise. Supervisor Rosenberg asked about gaps in service; Senholtz indicated rental assistance typically runs out by end of October. The committee raised the loss of AmeriCorps funding and Senholtz confirmed it is gone entirely.

discussions.item: United Way of Marathon County / 211 Services - 2027 Budget Presentation
discussions.body: Ben Lee presented 211 operations, noting the service covers nine counties and is on pace to exceed 2025 call volumes due to increased income support and assistance calls and the Ringle tornado response. He described how 211 data directly informs United Way's $2.1 million in annual community investments, citing child care and food pantry access as examples where data-driven investments shifted community outcomes. Administrator Leonard noted the county's annual 211 contract is $40,000, also planned to remain flat. Lee highlighted new rural outreach efforts including the Athens Caring Circle food pantry, which arose from 211 zip code data identifying unmet need.

discussions.item: ADRC of Central Wisconsin - Levy Request and Budget Update
discussions.body: Executive Director Mike Ray reported that nutrition program costs have risen nearly 50% over five years while funding has remained flat, forcing service reductions including cutting home-delivered meals from five to four per week for highest-need clients and three per week for moderate-need clients. The ADRC requested a $41,000 levy increase, which Administrator Leonard confirmed is already built into the 2027 budget draft; all four member counties must agree to the increase. Ray noted the Older Americans Act has not been reauthorized in nearly four years and Wisconsin provides only $650,000 statewide for nutrition programs compared to Minnesota's roughly $11 million. Supervisor Rosenberg suggested the committee consider passing resolutions advocating for increased state and federal funding. Ray also noted the ADRC's food vendor contract for Marathon, Lincoln, and Langlade counties is going out for RFP imminently and he hopes competitive bidding will help control costs.

discussions.item: 5B: Discussion and Possible Action to Forward to County Board - PFAS Well Sampling and Mobile Crisis
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson (identified as John in transcript) raised two items: the need to expand mobile crisis services beyond business hours, and an emerging PFAS-related well sampling grant opportunity through the DNR's PAS trust fund ($131 million pool). He noted the village of Maine area near the Greystone 3M facility has some of the state's highest PFAS readings and no current coordinated sampling. Robinson indicated grant proposals may be released in late September or October with an initial six-month award window and a 20% match that could be met with in-kind services. Chair Boots committed to discussing with Administrator Leonard and potentially scheduling a presentation at the next meeting, and asked Robinson to keep the committee apprised of DNR developments. The chair noted the topic needed to be formally agendized before further discussion.

discussions.item: 6A: Homelessness Response Foundational Framework - Quarterly Update
discussions.body: Public Health Coordinator Megan Barnett delivered her quarter-three update, reporting progress across four foundational framework focus areas: a steering committee has been formed with city and county leadership, a standardized intake form collecting uniform population data launched August 10th, a 5-year strategic planning session with 50-plus partners is scheduled for October, and 16 key informant interviews with people experiencing homelessness have been completed to inform the plan. She reported 25% of WMC intake data from last year showed out-of-county residents (primarily Milwaukee, Madison, and Chicago), and confirmed at least two individuals were recently dropped off at Bridge Street Mission by Lincoln County law enforcement. Supervisor Rosenberg raised the question of communities petitioning the state attorney general regarding unlawful transport of unhoused individuals; Administrator Leonard explained a legal opinion has been requested, likely by Eau Claire, and outlined the Chapter 51 transfer process. Supervisor Conway praised the framework as exactly what the county board had asked for. Barnett also highlighted recent community wins: 15 Bridge Street Mission residents secured jobs, the Mong American Center and Open Door landed a grant for two 15-passenger vans for second and third shift transportation, and the first 'Stability Starts Here' multi-agency service expo was held at the community partners campus.

discussions.item: 6B: Strategic Plan Survey Update
discussions.body: Chair Boots summarized results of 35 survey responses (roughly half from county board members, half from department heads) identifying top strategic plan priorities. 'Healthiest' and 'Safest' categories ranked highest overall. He noted 19 strategic objectives will go to the community for input, with a 20th to be added regarding preservation of agricultural land, added in part due to community interest around wind and solar development. He committed to emailing the full list to supervisors and presenting to other committees in October.

discussions.body: The committee tentatively agreed to add a tour of Bridge Street Mission following the September 30th meeting. Barnett agreed to coordinate with Bridge Street Mission to confirm the date. Ben Lee also highlighted that 47% of Marathon County residents 55 and older do not have enough to get by per the ALICE report, and urged a coordinated county and nonprofit advocacy effort for aging-related funding, noting Representative Schneider is authoring a bill for increased 211 funding.

title: Utility Committee Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Village Utility Committee held its September 1, 2026 meeting covering financial reports for both water and sewer utilities, a staffing update, ongoing lift station construction delays with liquidated damages, and several policy discussions including a water tower cell lease renewal with AT&T, a septic/holding tank request from Northland Lutheran High School, data center ordinance planning, and the proposed county highway garage project. The committee approved the AT&T water tower lease renewal and directed staff to invite Northland Lutheran representatives to a future meeting to advance discussion on a possible ordinance amendment allowing seasonal holding tanks.

Roll Call
Public Comment

discussions.item: Utility Director Report
discussions.body: Utility Director Greg reported that lift station 2 panel installation is scheduled for the following Wednesday after WPS installed the wrong transformer. He also reported that a water department employee gave two weeks notice, requiring the position to be posted, and that the 2027 budget will include a request for an additional utility department employee due to growth and treatment plant demands. Green Bay Python TV is performing televising and cleaning of manholes on Kowalski Road.

discussions.item: Lift Station 8 Construction Delays and Liquidated Damages
discussions.body: Lift station 8 remains visually incomplete with the original substantial completion date of July 15 having passed. The contractor now estimates completion by end of September, though committee members expressed skepticism. Liquidated damages of $500 per day are being imposed on the contractor covering the entire project scope, including boring under Highway 51/52 and connection to lift station 7. Approximately 35% of the roughly $2.4 million contract remains unpaid, giving the village leverage.

discussions.item: Financial Report - Water and Sewer Utility Funds
discussions.body: Finance staff reported water utility revenues through seven months at $450,000 versus $449,000 last year, with operational expenses at $282,000 versus $261,000 — essentially flat. The sewer utility showed a $121,000 surplus versus $268,000 last year, with expenses at $559,000 versus $414,000, driven largely by Remote Metro Sewage District charges of $324,000 compared to $216,000 the prior year. Discussion centered on whether the elevated Remote Metro costs reflect a new normal due to infiltration from a wet spring, and whether rate adjustments will be needed in 2027. General obligation debt capacity stands at 17% used with $49 million available; staff discussed scenarios for upcoming sewer utility borrowing using either revenue bonds or general obligation debt pending completion of the 2025 audit.

discussions.item: Water Tower AT&T Cell Lease Agreement
discussions.body: The committee reviewed a proposed five-year lease agreement with AT&T for antenna space on the village water tower at $27,000 in year one with a 2% annual escalator, down from the most recent payment of $35,123 and previous years' rate of $31,360. One committee member (Alex Fedwick) voted no, expressing concern that insufficient time was spent negotiating a better rate, while others acknowledged the need to move forward. The motion passed 4-1.

discussions.item: Septic Tank/Holding Tank Ordinance - Northland Lutheran High School
discussions.body: Greg explained that Northland Lutheran High School has sought approval for a holding tank near their athletic fields' concession stand for approximately 18 months, initially with informal encouragement from former development director Peter Wagner who is no longer with the village. The current ordinance prohibits septic tanks within the sewage district. Committee members expressed willingness to work with the school but raised concerns about opening the door to other applicants and noted the need for strict, narrow ordinance language covering seasonal use, non-residential nature, distance requirements, and tank size limits. The committee directed staff to invite Northland Lutheran representatives, including their plumber, to the next utility committee meeting.

discussions.item: Data Center Ordinance Discussion
discussions.body: The committee discussed the village board's one-year moratorium on data center approvals and the need for utility-side input on what regulations to pursue over the next 12 months. Key concerns included water consumption limits, requirements for closed-loop cooling systems, sewer discharge capacity, and the difficulty of identifying data center customers before projects are finalized. Committee members noted the wide range of data center sizes and that high water and power consumers could mask their identity as industrial customers. No action was taken; the committee agreed to continue researching ordinances from other municipalities.

discussions.item: County Highway Garage Update
discussions.body: Greg reported that SD Ellenbacker is ready to begin construction on the county highway garage pending state plan approval, which could come any day or take several more weeks. The contractor is seeking preliminary approval just for the foundation to begin work before cold weather. Discussion also addressed the garage's planned use of a private well for brine-making operations, with committee member Craig Mortensen raising detailed concerns about salt runoff contaminating groundwater given historical problems at other county facilities, and recommending the village review the stormwater and drainage plan for the site.

title: Economic Development Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Economic Development Committee met on September 15, 2025, covering several significant development matters including survey results for the contaminated 1300 Cleveland Avenue site, a proposed mixed-use development agreement with Wangard for the Riverlife South project, and an early-stage public housing expansion proposal from the CDA. The Wangard development agreement failed to pass after a 2-1 vote, while the committee directed staff to schedule a green team meeting with the DNR and prepare a formal deed restriction formalizing non-industrial use of the Cleveland Avenue property.
