discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Four members of the public spoke. Colleen Armstrong, owner of property adjacent to the proposed Eminent Development Corporation site at Second Street and 2011 East Bridge Street, said she received no formal notification about the multi-story mixed-use project and demanded the city explain the oversight and pause the agreement until a neighborhood meeting is held. Tom Kian, identified as the neighborhood representative for the Cleveland Avenue project, urged the committee to ensure remediation is done concurrently with redevelopment rather than in advance, and asked that the new comprehensive plan formally reflect a non-industrial future land use for the property. Drew Wowski expressed support for accelerating Cleveland Avenue development, noting survey respondents favored green space and community amenities paired with housing. Becky Hda, a Cleveland Avenue-area resident, read directly from the survey's open-ended responses to emphasize that neighbors overwhelmingly want contamination cleanup before any other decisions are made.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes from July 7th Economic Development Committee Meeting
discussions.body: A motion was made by Alder Kilian and seconded by Alder Lukans to approve the minutes. The vote passed unanimously with no opposition noted.

discussions.item: Survey Results for 1300 Cleveland Avenue
discussions.body: Assistant City Planner Carrie Edmonson presented results from 39 completed surveys following a May 28 neighborhood meeting. The top preferred non-industrial land use was a community center or senior center, followed by active outdoor recreation; a majority supported integrating housing if it enabled funding of preferred uses. Alder Kilian directed staff to schedule a green team meeting with the DNR before the next ED meeting to discuss remediation funding and align cleanup plans with development, and called for a formal deed restriction or resolution cementing non-industrial status for the property. The chair agreed and directed staff to bring a deed restriction proposal to the next meeting. Alder Neil emphasized that remediation depth is project-specific and that the city has previously committed to remediating to residential standards. Alder Lukans requested a cost breakdown for remediation under different development scenarios. No vote was taken on this item as it was informational with direction given to staff.

discussions.item: East Thomas Street and McClary Street RFI Update
discussions.body: Economic Development Manager Patrick reported that no formal proposals were received after the RFI was released in April, though informal discussions continue with entities including Habitat for Humanity. Staff recommended keeping the RFI open to allow continued negotiations and marketing. Alder Kilian noted approximately $600,000 in ARPA funds had been transferred to the CDA for infill housing. The committee voted unanimously to keep the RFI open and continue marketing the sites.

discussions.item: Development Agreement with Wangard for Riverlife South Project
discussions.body: Director Fifick presented a development agreement for 920 North First Street and 15 Fulton Street, translating the previously approved term sheet into a binding contract. Key terms include the developer purchasing city land for $100,000, a total anticipated development cost of $36.1 million, and the developer receiving 80% of new property tax generated via pay-as-you-go TIF reimbursement up to $4.84 million over a maximum of 17 years, with a 5.75% interest rate and a maximum total reimbursement of $8.35 million plus a look-back provision. Isaac from Quarles confirmed the material terms matched the approved term sheet. Alder Kilian stated she had never supported the project and would vote no. Alder Neil moved to approve, stating the numbers make sense and he could find no negatives. The motion was seconded by Alder Lukans. The vote resulted in two in favor and one opposed (Alder Kilian), with the chair also voting no, causing the motion to fail as it did not achieve a majority.

discussions.item: Proposed Meeting Time Change
discussions.body: The committee discussed moving the meeting start time from 5:15 to 5:30 p.m. The chair relayed that absent committee member Alder Tierney had communicated she was fine with 5:15 but not earlier. The motion to change the meeting time passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Accepting Donation of 313 North 1st Avenue Property
discussions.body: Director Fifick explained the 0.06-acre parcel, located behind Bridge Street Mission, was being donated by former owners MBX after the city's attorney's office worked through the chain of title. Alder Kilian raised concerns about potential contamination given the property's prior use as an ice and fuel company, and questioned whether a phase one or phase two environmental assessment had been done. The chair noted the property has no road access and is essentially a lawn strip between two residential properties, suggesting possible sale to an adjacent owner. Despite contamination concerns, the committee voted to accept the donation.

discussions.item: Wausau CDA Proposed New Public Housing Development
discussions.body: CDA Assistant Director Julie Burkinmeer presented an early-stage proposal to develop 18 to 64 new public housing units by repositioning the CDA's existing 46 scattered-site units to a Section 18 project-based voucher funding model, freeing up HUD Faircloth units for new construction. She emphasized the extreme demand—the wait list for the CDA's single one-bedroom unit is over five years—and that rents would remain income-based at 30% of household income. The proposed development would be in one consolidated location rather than scattered sites, requiring at least one acre. No specific site has been identified yet. The CDA board is expected to consider the repositioning plan in October. No vote was taken; this was an informational presentation.

title: Water Works Commission Meeting
overview: The Wausau Water Works Commission met on September 1, 2026, primarily to receive a detailed financial presentation from Brian Ramer of Ehlers on long-range cash flow projections and potential rate adjustments for both the water and wastewater utilities. The commission heard that the water utility is currently about 13% rate-deficient under PSC math, with deficiency growing to 20% by 2027 if no action is taken, and received an update on a PFAS exceedance detected in wastewater effluent. No formal rate decisions were made; staff indicated they would bring the rate discussion back next month for a possible decision.

discussions.item: Minutes of August 12th Meeting
discussions.body: A motion was made by Galire and seconded by Martins to approve the minutes of the August 12th meeting. There was no discussion. The motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Director's Report - Wastewater Project Updates
discussions.body: Staff reported that the Cherry Street project is essentially complete with one punch list item remaining, to be addressed on-site Thursday. The Headworks Screening project remains ongoing with a substantial completion deadline of October 15 and final completion of November 15. The Crocker Street Lift Station project was noted as new, with a pre-construction meeting scheduled for September 2nd. No questions were raised by commission members.

discussions.item: Ehlers Financial Presentation - Water Utility Rate Analysis
discussions.body: Brian Ramer of Ehlers presented a 10-year financial forecast for the water utility, explaining that under PSC math the utility is currently about 7.3% rate-deficient for 2026, growing to approximately 13% now and 20% by August 2027 if no action is taken. He outlined three options: do nothing (infeasible), use simplified rate adjustments of 3% in 2027 and 2028 followed by a 16% conventional rate case, or file a conventional rate case sooner yielding approximately a 14% adjustment. Commission member Hadley questioned how approximately $5 million in PFAS lawsuit proceeds (PAS funds) and the payment-in-lieu-of-taxes (pilot) would affect rate calculations; Ramer explained the PSC has not consistently reduced rate adjustments based on lawsuit proceeds and that reducing the pilot would lower the rate adjustment but create a general fund revenue gap. Martins asked about the timeline for filing, and Ramer confirmed the commission has until July 31, 2027 before the PSC math resets. Staff director Eric noted the commission had previously expressed interest in monthly billing and tiered rate structures for low-volume users, and recommended a small rate increase for 2027 with planning for a larger rate case in 2028 or 2029. No vote was taken; the director indicated the matter would return next month for a possible decision.

discussions.item: Ehlers Financial Presentation - Sewer Utility Rate Analysis
discussions.body: Ramer presented the sewer utility financial outlook, noting debt coverage has been creeping back toward minimum thresholds and that the last rate adjustment was April 1, 2023. He recommended small, more frequent inflationary rate adjustments — using 4% as an illustrative example — which would increase an average residential quarterly sewer bill by approximately $4.30. Unlike the water utility, the sewer utility is not regulated by the PSC and the commission has full authority to set rates. No vote was taken.

discussions.item: PFAS Monitoring Update - Wastewater Effluent
discussions.body: Ben Brooks reported that the first compliance-required effluent sample taken May 7th returned a PFOS level of 9.44 parts per trillion, above the proposed limit of 8 parts per trillion, which he described as unexpected given prior favorable readings. Staff has reviewed sampling protocols and found no evidence of cross-contamination, concluding the PFAS is entering the system from external sources. Brooks indicated plans to test collection system locations to identify the contamination source and noted the commission may need to consider amending the city sewer ordinance to require testing by large industrial users. Biosolids results were noted as favorable; an additional biosolids test is planned to establish compliance under the permit effective May 1st. Commission members raised no formal objections; the item was informational.

discussions.item: WDNR Response to 2025 Compliance Maintenance Annual Report
discussions.body: Brooks reported that the DNR's response letter to the 2025 annual compliance report was entirely positive, with all grade A ratings. The DNR commended the utility for properly reporting a sanitary sewer overflow (SSO) in September 2024 and noted the utility cleaned 48.9% of the collection system and televised 10%. The DNR letter stated the utility met all requirements and encouraged staff to keep up the good work.

title: Parks and Recreation Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Parks and Recreation Committee met on August 31, 2026 and took action on several items including unanimously approving acceptance of a donated scoreboard for Memorial Park, unanimously recommending historic landmark designation for Yaki Park, approving amendments to Chapter 2 of the city's comprehensive plan addressing natural resources, and directing staff to paint a centerline on the River Edge Trail. The committee also received and debated a detailed 2027 department budget overview that included proposals for pool staffing reductions, dock consolidation, and a potential urban forestry fee, with no final budget votes taken but significant discussion about the financial sustainability of city pools and other park amenities.

Consideration of Minutes from July 6, 2026 Regular Meeting

discussions.item: Public Comment – Yaki Park Historic Designation
discussions.body: Kathy Foley, former director of the Leigh Yawkey Woodson Art Museum, spoke on behalf of five Yawkey heirs — great-grandchildren of Cyrus Yawkey — reading a signed statement expressing full support for designating Yaki Park as a historic landmark. Foley noted the park is 106 years old and deeded for public use in perpetuity. She left the signed statement for the committee record.

discussions.item: Minutes Approval – July 6, 2026 Meeting
discussions.body: The chair asked for any corrections to the minutes of the July 6, 2026 regular meeting. With none offered, Alder Slonsky moved to approve and Alder Lukans seconded. The minutes were approved unanimously.

discussions.item: 3A: Scoreboard Donation at Memorial Park
discussions.body: Parks staff (identified as Jamie) explained that Wausau Youth Baseball is funding the entire scoreboard donation, which replaces an old Pepsi-branded board. No sponsor has been secured yet; if one is found, it would require approval through the parks office per the sponsorship policy. The item came before the committee due to the scoreboard's 15-to-20-year lifespan exceeding the threshold requiring committee review even though the cost is under $5,000. Alder Slonsky moved to accept the donation, Alder Neil seconded, and it passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 3B: Yaki Park Historical Landmark Designation
discussions.body: Staff clarified that the designation applies only to the park grounds — including the colonnade and fountain — not to the Yawkey family home located a block away. City staff member Brad explained that as a landmark, the historic preservation commission would have binding authority (not merely advisory) over any substantial changes to the park. Staff noted that if the city ever ceased to use the property as public space, it reverts to the Yawkey family per the deed. A public hearing at the Historic Preservation Commission is set for September 23, followed by plan commission and ultimately city council approval. Alder Troub moved to adopt the designation, Alder Slonsky seconded, and it passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 3C: Natural Resources Chapter 2 – Comprehensive Plan Review
discussions.body: City planner Carrie Edmonson and parks staff presented proposed updates to Chapter 2, informed heavily by the City of Madison's comprehensive plan and work with city forester John Kahhan. Committee members proposed several additions: Alder Lukans raised concerns about pesticide drift, native plantings, and the environmental impacts of artificial turf with crumb rubber infill; Alder Slonsky requested strengthening language around restoring damaged wetlands from 'consider developing' to a firmer commitment; Alder Troub raised the need to address native grasses and lawn alternatives in parks and residential areas; Alder Lukans also raised light pollution as it relates to bird habitat. Alder Neil moved to approve Chapter 2 as presented with the new feedback incorporated, Alder Slonsky seconded, and the motion passed unanimously. The chapter next goes to plan commission and then city council.

discussions.item: 3D: Painting a Centerline Lane on the River Edge Trail
discussions.body: Alder Neil proposed painting a broken centerline stripe on the River Edge Trail from Winton to Oak Island, citing a successful example in Marquette, Michigan and safety benefits for mixed-use path users. Alder Troub supported the idea but emphasized the need for accompanying signage such as 'keep right except to pass,' noting that lines alone may be ignored without reinforcement. Alder Slonsky expressed mild hesitation about creating the appearance of an enforceable rule that would not actually be enforced. Staff noted a prior example of painting 'slow, children present' markings near a playground that appeared to reduce complaints. Alder Troub moved to proceed with painting the line using city staff on staff's own timeline to avoid additional costs, with a cost report back to the committee for future budget planning; Alder Neil seconded. The motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 3E: 2027 Department Budget Overview and Proposed Changes
discussions.body: Parks Director Jamie presented a budget built to the mayor's directive of a flat 'cost of doing business' increase, coming in at approximately 1% over last year. The largest proposed cost-reduction measure was rotating pool closures across the three aquatic centers to reduce staffing costs; the department spends $449,000 on pools annually with only a 19% cost recovery rate. Two pool rotation options were presented — one keeping two pools open five days a week with all three open on weekends, and one closing all three pools one day per week for higher savings of approximately $29,781. Committee members generally favored keeping all three pools open Saturday and Sunday. Other proposals included reducing warf docks from seven to three (consolidating into a wider central platform), pausing goat use on Barker Stewart Island for one year with mowing as an alternative, switching from tablet to liquid chlorine in bulk, reducing the small projects budget by $5,000, and adding a $2-per-household-per-month urban forestry fee. Alder Troub strongly opposed the urban forestry fee as an additional burden on taxpayers already funding forestry through the property tax levy; Alder Slonsky expressed interest in exploring it but acknowledged its regressive nature for single-family homeowners. No formal votes were taken on budget items; the committee was asked to provide direction to staff on which operational changes to include in the budget submission to the mayor.

title: Special Village Board Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Village Board held a special meeting on August 27, 2026, with one primary action item: accepting the resignation of Village Clerk Jennifer Poyer, which passed 6-0. The meeting was preceded by pointed public comment from three residents criticizing the board over two costly workplace investigations totaling $105,000, vague closed session notices, and broader governance concerns. Trustee Stowell was absent.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Three residents spoke critically of the village board. Bruny Kramer of 2150 E. State Hwy 153 criticized a pattern of poor governance over the past six months, referencing a mining situation and excessive closed sessions, and suggested board members seek training. Chris Johnson of 1998 Woodgate Lane delivered an extended rebuke, alleging that a workplace investigation costing approximately $40,000 was rooted in ego between President Joling and former administrator Sorenson, that closed session notices were improperly vague, and that employee privacy was mishandled through inadequate redactions; Johnson also addressed an apparent comment made about her Facebook posts before the meeting, calling it unprofessional. Guy Fredl of 2240 Ruby Drive, identifying himself as a longtime village volunteer, presented specific cost figures—$60,000 for a first investigation by Von Briesen and Roper and $45,000 for a second, totaling $105,000—and noted the village had lost three employees and three female board members in recent years, warning of potential litigation from Peter Wagner and Jennifer Poyer and suggesting the village hire a contracted HR professional to handle such matters.

discussions.item: Acceptance of Clerk's Resignation
discussions.body: The board voted 6-0 to accept the resignation of Village Clerk Jennifer Poyer as submitted. Following the vote, a trustee—identified in the transcript as raising additional comments—asked that staff coordinate a transition plan covering return of village property, system and social media passwords, and a status report from Poyer on outstanding work items. The same trustee thanked Poyer for her work on community events, social media, and elections, and wished her well. President Joling noted the village may need to call an additional meeting if an interim clerk is secured.

title: Board Regular Meeting Pt.2
overview: The Marathon County Board met to address the Hub City Wind project resolution from the Executive Committee, which lacked a concrete 'therefore be it resolved' clause. After extensive debate, the board voted to refer the matter back to the Executive Committee for a clearer recommendation, with supervisors expressing frustration over procedural issues and the county's limited authority to constrain the project given state PSC jurisdiction over large wind projects.

discussions.item: Hub City Wind Project Resolution – Procedural Objection
discussions.body: Vice Chair Chris Dickinson raised an immediate procedural objection, arguing the resolution was invalid because it contained no 'therefore be it resolved' clause — effectively resolving nothing. Corp Counsel confirmed the resolution was intentionally written that way to allow the board to amend it in whatever direction they chose. Dickinson called this unprecedented in his experience and expressed concern about setting a bad procedural precedent.

discussions.item: Motion to Refer Back to Executive Committee
discussions.body: Dickinson moved to refer the matter back to the Executive Committee to develop a concrete recommendation and bring it to the September board meeting. Supervisor Caravelli supported the referral, noting the item had been confusing even at the Thursday discussion. Vice Chair Boots explained she had brought it to the full board so all 38 supervisors could weigh in, but expressed no objection to referring it back.

discussions.item: Robinson Amendment (Not Voted On)
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson described a proposed amendment that would direct the County Administrator to send Alliant Energy the Alternative Energy Project Local Impact Advisory Committee report and request a contractual response addressing community concerns by October 1st. Corp Counsel ruled this amendment was not germane to the motion to refer and therefore out of order while the referral motion was on the floor. Robinson noted the 180-day PSC application window made timely action important.

discussions.item: Moratorium Debate and PSC Jurisdiction
discussions.body: Multiple supervisors including Gaul, Hagan, Hopper, and Sendelbach advocated for a moratorium, citing constituent demand and the project's unprecedented tower height of 620 feet. Corp Counsel and Rebecca (a PSC representative on the line) clarified repeatedly that while the county could legally pass a moratorium, the PSC is not required to consider it for projects over 100 MW, rendering it largely symbolic. Supervisor Gaul pushed for the board to investigate formal intervention in the PSC process as an alternative approach.

discussions.item: Vote to End Debate and Refer to Executive Committee
discussions.body: Supervisor Ritter called the previous question, which was seconded by Supervisor Krebs. The motion to end debate passed, though not unanimously. The board then voted on the referral motion, which also carried but was not unanimous. The matter will return to the Executive Committee for a recommendation before coming back to the full board.

publicComment: No public comment was offered during this portion of the meeting, though supervisors referenced extensive prior public input with multiple speakers noting that over 90% of constituents at prior meetings opposed the Hub City Wind project or a joint development agreement with Alliant Energy.
